digest.definition: The study of the human capacity for language in every mode, spoken, signed and written: its structure, its processing in the mind and brain, and how it is acquired, used, interpreted and changes in social, cultural and historical settings
distinctiveFeatures: The study of the human capacity for language in every mode, spoken, signed and written: its structure, its processing in the mind and brain, and how it is acquired, used, interpreted and changes in social, cultural and historical settings
Its guiding principle is that linguistic behaviour can be explained by systematic study, with theoretical models tested against empirical data, by both cognitive and social approaches
Broad and interdisciplinary, spanning the sciences, social sciences and humanities; the statement keeps the subject's boundaries deliberately open and evolving

Taught through levels of analysis (phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics) applied to domains of language use and to applied fields such as clinical, computational and forensic linguistics, language teaching and lexicography
Reflexive and socially engaged: students examine their own linguistic identities and attitudes, and the subject studies language, power and social hierarchy and works in partnership with communities
Commonly studied in combination, with English, TESOL, other languages, psychology, philosophy, politics and many more; single honours covers most of the content, joint routes a selection

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: EDI sits inside the subject knowledge itself: comparative study of unrelated, often non-European languages, attention to vernaculars, minority languages and representation, reflexivity about one's own language attitudes, and research done with communities; assessment linked to real-life EDI issues (D1, 1.7 to 1.11); threshold items on ideology, power and minority groups and a generic skill on EDI at work (D1, 4.5, 4.6)

an inclusive view of all modes of language, sign included; accessible formats and reasonable adjustments; multilingual home backgrounds as a resource; provider awareness of disabled students' needs and accessible digital content (D1, 1.12 to 1.16); resourcing accessible delivery and uneven access to technology (D1, 2.11, 2.12)

headed Sustainability: language as central to articulating sustainable futures; links to UNESCO's goals SDG4, SDG5, SDG8 and SDG16; discourse analysis of climate communication; endangered-language and documentation work opening space for other knowledges (D1, 1.17 to 1.21); SDG themes in assessment (D1, 3.11); a threshold item and two generic skills (D1, 4.5, 4.6)

enterprise and entrepreneurship education for careers and wider social value, placements and external links; the subject's critical, creative and analytical mix; IT and data skills; graduates sought in publishing, technology, AI, teaching, therapy, data science and more (D1, 1.22 to 1.31); employability among the debates in the generic skills (D1, 4.6)

transferable.text: You will have the chance to practise forming hypotheses and testing them, a skill employers value.
You will build your ability to weigh up competing theories and explanations, which employers value.
You will practise communicating in speech, in other non-verbal ways and with visuals, choosing a format that suits your audience.
You will learn to design experiments and to plan and carry out research projects, on your own and with others.
You will come to understand how to use evidence and data properly and ethically.
You will build your ability to judge competing theories and explanations, and the evidence behind each.
You will learn to tell the difference between a system for describing language and the language data itself.
You will practise drawing out and combining information and gathering, analysing and working with many kinds of data.
You will build your skill in reading and making sense of diagrams, tables and graphs.
You will learn to find and combine information from many kinds of source and to credit and list your sources properly.
You will build your ability to study and learn well on your own.
You will come to understand why health and safety, and equality, diversity and inclusion, matter in a workplace.
You will have the chance to take part in current debates about sustainability, careers and global perspectives, including decolonisation and anti-racism.
You will come to see why acting sustainably and behaving ethically matter, and practise both.
You will practise explaining what you know about language, clearly and sensitively, to people who make policies where language matters.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Linguistics Degree

statements.about: professional communication across settings, respecting diversity
statements.paraphrase: Linguistics students work in many settings and are normally expected to grow in their ability to communicate professionally while respecting linguistic, social and cultural diversity; they are also helped to become active, confident and independent learners.

forPractitioner.text: Plan for a steady growth in professional communication across the course, set in varied environments, with respect for linguistic, social and cultural difference built in; support students to learn actively and independently and to read their academic setting critically.

forBeneficiary.text: Over your course you are normally expected to get better at communicating in a professional way, wherever you are working, while showing respect for differences of language, society and culture. You will also be helped to learn actively and on your own, with growing confidence.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Linguistics Degree

statements.appliesTo: those who design and deliver education
statements.about: attention to linguistic diversity for inclusive education (SDG4)
statements.paraphrase: Using, analysing and understanding language underpins empowerment, inclusion and fair access, so language and linguistic diversity should receive particular attention in any effort to make education inclusive for everyone (SDG4, Quality Education).

forPractitioner.text: Give language and linguistic diversity deliberate attention when making education inclusive: language use and understanding shape who gains access, inclusion and opportunity, in line with SDG4 (Quality Education).

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a principle for those who shape education, not an outcome a student reaches

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Linguistics Degree

statements.about: explaining and showing skills to employers
statements.paraphrase: The curriculum builds skills with real social reach, such as questioning language ideologies, scrutinising institutional policy, exposing hidden assumptions in discourse and weighing theories against data; graduates are able to explain and show these skills, and other useful personal attributes, to employers.

forPractitioner.text: Make the social uses of linguistic skill visible in modules (challenging language ideologies, scrutinising policy, uncovering assumptions in discourse, testing theory against data) and give students practice in naming and evidencing those skills for employers.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to explain to employers, and show them, the skills your study has given you: questioning beliefs about language, examining how institutions use it, spotting hidden assumptions and judging theories against evidence.

statements.about: progression through levels to the honours threshold
statements.paraphrase: On an honours degree (FHEQ Level 6; FQHEIS Level 10) students will move from one level of study to the next under each institution's rules, and each level is expected to add knowledge, skills, expertise and experience that lead to meeting the threshold subject skills.

forPractitioner.text: Map each level of the course so that it adds knowledge, skills, expertise and experience in steps that lead to the threshold subject skills at the end; progression rules remain the institution's own.

forBeneficiary.text: You will move up through the levels of your course under your institution's rules, and each year should build what you know and can do until you reach the standard needed for your honours degree.

statements.appliesTo: students on combined, joint or major-minor routes
statements.about: core subject skills on joint and combined routes
statements.paraphrase: Students on combined, joint or major-minor routes will reach the core parts of the subject's specific and generic skills and will add others that their joint course requires; they may also study where the two subjects overlap.

forPractitioner.text: On joint, combined or major-minor routes, secure the core of the subject's specific and generic skills, then let the partner subject's requirements add to them; consider space for interdisciplinary study across the two.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study linguistics with another subject, you will gain the core linguistics skills, both subject-specific and general, and add others that your other subject asks for. You may also get to explore where the two subjects meet.

statements.paraphrase: As funding models change, providers will more and more need to consider standalone micro-credentials that can count towards larger awards; these need to attract students for professional and personal growth and to add to the study of the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Consider short standalone credentials that can stack into larger awards, designed so they appeal to learners for professional and personal development and still advance the study of linguistics.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a forecast about provider planning, not something a student achieves

statements.appliesTo: providers delivering accessible, inclusive and flexible content
statements.about: resourcing accessible delivery and uneven access to technology
statements.paraphrase: Accessible, inclusive and flexible content requires suitable resources and staff training to keep quality consistent, and where courses use digital technology, students' unequal access to it needs to be recognised so that no one is disadvantaged.

forPractitioner.text: Resource and train staff for accessible, inclusive and flexible delivery; where you use digital technology, account for students' differing access to devices and connectivity so that none is disadvantaged.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect

statements.paraphrase: Externality is essential to UK quality assurance: providers will bring external reviewers into periodic review for an outside view of proposed changes and to make sure threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Involve external reviewers in periodic review, asking them to test proposed changes, confirm that threshold standards are met and judge whether content fits the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in quality assurance

statements.about: using Annex D to judge achievement above threshold
statements.paraphrase: Most students will do clearly better than the minimum threshold; each provider decides what counts as evidence of that and should refer to Annex D, which describes the four honours classifications (1st, 2.1, 2.2 and 3rd) for FHEQ Level 6 and FQHEIS Level 10.

forPractitioner.text: Set your own evidence for achievement above the threshold, and use Annex D, which describes each honours class at FHEQ Level 6 (FQHEIS Level 10), when you describe the 1st, 2.1, 2.2 and 3rd.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student-facing account of classes belongs to the provider's own criteria

statements.appliesTo: graduates with a bachelor's degree in the subject
statements.about: core areas of analysis and the domains of language
statements.paraphrase: Graduates will be expected to grasp the basic ideas and analytic methods of the core areas, from phonetics to discourse, a foundation for substantial knowledge of the domains where language systems arise, such as acquisition, variation and change, language in society and language as a cognitive object.

forPractitioner.text: Ensure every graduate meets the basic concepts and analytic methods of the core areas (phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics and discourse), then builds on them into domains such as acquisition, variation and change, society and cognition.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be expected to understand the basic ideas and methods of analysis in the core areas of linguistics, such as sounds, word structure, sentence structure, meaning, use in context and discourse, and to use them to learn about how language is acquired, varies, changes, works in society and works in the mind.

statements.paraphrase: A graduate is expected to know a range of empirical language phenomena and the technical terms and methods used to describe and analyse them; this knowledge may be mainly descriptive but usually rests on a suitable theoretical framework.

forPractitioner.text: Expose students to a range of real language phenomena and to the terminology and methods for describing and analysing them, framed by theory even where the work is mostly descriptive.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to know about a range of real language phenomena and the technical terms and methods used to describe and analyse them, usually within a theory that explains them.

statements.about: fundamental analytical concepts and methods of inquiry
statements.paraphrase: Show knowledge of the basic analytic concepts and methods of inquiry that a linguistics degree calls for.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold show they know the field's basic analytic concepts and its methods of inquiry.

forBeneficiary.text: You will show that you know the basic concepts linguists use to analyse language and the main ways they investigate it.

statements.paraphrase: Approach language phenomena systematically: identifying, describing and then analysing them.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold identify, describe and analyse language phenomena in an orderly, systematic way.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to work through language data step by step: spotting a feature, describing it and then analysing it.

statements.paraphrase: Pose well-grounded questions about how language is structured and used.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold pose well-grounded questions about language structure and use.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to ask good, well-reasoned questions about how language is built and how people use it.

statements.about: basic data collection, elicitation and transcription
statements.paraphrase: Use the basic methods for gathering or eliciting and transcribing data that suit the different branches of linguistics, from corpora and media texts to elicitation, introspection, experiments, questionnaires, interviews and fieldwork.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold apply basic techniques for collecting or eliciting and transcribing data suited to the sub-disciplines, such as corpora, media and political or advertising texts, elicitation tasks, introspection, laboratory work, questionnaires, interviews or fieldwork.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to use the basic ways of gathering and transcribing language data that fit your area, such as corpora, media texts, experiments, questionnaires, interviews or fieldwork.

statements.about: level-specific analytical concepts applied to data
statements.paraphrase: Use the analytic concepts belonging to each level of linguistic analysis on suitable sets of data.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold apply the analytic concepts of each level of linguistic analysis to suitable data sets.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to take the concepts for each level of analysis, such as sounds, words or sentences, and use them on real data.

statements.paraphrase: Draw linguistic generalisations and build and test hypotheses within linguistics, using fitting evidence.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold formulate linguistic generalisations and construct and test hypotheses on suitable evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to draw general patterns from language data and set up and test hypotheses using the right kind of evidence.

statements.paraphrase: Weigh competing analyses of a data set, understanding how theories shape analysis and decide what counts as evidence.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold evaluate alternative analyses of a data set, understanding how theory organises analysis and settles what counts as evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to compare different analyses of the same data and judge between them, knowing how theory shapes analysis and what counts as evidence.

statements.paraphrase: Weigh competing theories, drawing on what linguistic theory is and on what counts as an explanation in linguistics.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold evaluate alternative theories, grounded in an understanding of linguistic theory and of explanation in the field.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to compare and judge rival theories, knowing what a linguistic theory is and what makes a good explanation.

statements.paraphrase: Set out linguistic data and analysis with the methods and conventions of each sub-discipline, such as bracketing, tree diagrams, formal logic, graphs, tables, matrices and transcription systems.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold present data and analysis using each sub-discipline's conventions: bracketing, tree diagrams, formal logic, graphs, tables, matrices and transcription systems.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to set out your data and analysis using the conventions your area expects, such as tree diagrams, brackets, logic notation, graphs, tables or phonetic transcription.

statements.paraphrase: Bring linguistic terms, theory and research to bear on problems in the world beyond the discipline.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold use linguistic terminology, theory and research to tackle real-world problems.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to use linguistic terms, theory and research to help with real problems outside your course.

statements.paraphrase: Grasp, and explain to others, what can be observed about how language represents ideology, power, social identities and realities.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold understand and communicate observations on how language represents ideology, power, social identity and social reality.

forBeneficiary.text: You will understand, and be able to explain, how language can carry ideology and power and shape how identities and social realities are shown.

statements.paraphrase: Analyse how language represents minority groups across regional, sociocultural and situational settings.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold analyse how language depicts minority groups across regional, sociocultural and situational settings.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to analyse how language portrays minority groups in different places, cultures and situations.

statements.paraphrase: Find and investigate cases of language variation, and their causes, across situational, social, cultural, regional and historical contexts, including multilingual and cross-cultural ones.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold identify and examine examples of, and reasons for, variation across situational, social, cultural, regional, historical, multilingual and cross-cultural contexts.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to spot and look into how and why language varies between situations, social groups, cultures, regions and periods, as well as between languages.

statements.about: language's role in shaping norms and identities
statements.paraphrase: Judge how language helps shape sociocultural norms, identities and realities in public and private domains.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold evaluate how far language shapes sociocultural norms, identities and realities, in public and in private domains.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be able to judge how language helps to shape social norms, identities and realities, in public life and in private.

statements.about: language and ideology in global and sustainability contexts
statements.paraphrase: Show some grasp of how language use and beliefs about language bear on globalisation, mobility, sustainability and social justice.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates at threshold show some grasp of how language use and language ideologies connect with globalisation, mobility, sustainability and social justice.

forBeneficiary.text: You will show some understanding of how language use and beliefs about language connect with globalisation, migration and movement, sustainability and social justice.

statements.paraphrase: Forming hypotheses and testing them.

forPractitioner.text: Give students practice in forming hypotheses and testing them.

forBeneficiary.text: You will have the chance to practise forming hypotheses and testing them, a skill employers value.

statements.paraphrase: Judging the strengths of competing theories and explanations.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' ability to weigh the merits of contrasting theories and explanations.

forBeneficiary.text: You will build your ability to weigh up competing theories and explanations, which employers value.

statements.paraphrase: Communicating in spoken, non-verbal and graphic forms, in a format that suits the audience.

forPractitioner.text: Give practice in spoken, non-verbal and graphic communication, choosing the format for the audience.

forBeneficiary.text: You will practise communicating in speech, in other non-verbal ways and with visuals, choosing a format that suits your audience.

statements.about: research and experimental design, alone and in groups
statements.paraphrase: Designing experiments and designing and carrying out research projects, alone and in groups.

forPractitioner.text: Build experimental design and the design and conduct of research projects, both individual and group, into the course.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn to design experiments and to plan and carry out research projects, on your own and with others.

statements.about: ethical and appropriate use of evidence
statements.paraphrase: Knowing how to use evidence and data properly and ethically.

forPractitioner.text: Teach the proper and ethical use of evidence and data, including in students' own research.

forBeneficiary.text: You will come to understand how to use evidence and data properly and ethically.

statements.paraphrase: Judging the merits of contrasting theories and explanations and of the evidence for them.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' judgement of contrasting theories, explanations and the evidence behind them.

forBeneficiary.text: You will build your ability to judge competing theories and explanations, and the evidence behind each.

statements.about: telling descriptive systems apart from data
statements.paraphrase: Keeping apart a system of description and the data it is used to describe.

forPractitioner.text: Help students separate descriptive frameworks from the data they describe.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn to tell the difference between a system for describing language and the language data itself.

statements.about: handling information and data of many kinds
statements.paraphrase: Abstracting and combining information, and gathering, analysing and working with varied kinds of data.

forPractitioner.text: Give students practice in abstracting and synthesising information and in collecting, analysing and manipulating varied data.

forBeneficiary.text: You will practise drawing out and combining information and gathering, analysing and working with many kinds of data.

statements.paraphrase: Making sense of information shown in diagrams, tables and graphs.

forPractitioner.text: Build students' skill in interpreting diagrams, tables and graphs.

forBeneficiary.text: You will build your skill in reading and making sense of diagrams, tables and graphs.

statements.about: finding and combining sources with proper acknowledgement
statements.paraphrase: Tracking down and combining information from varied formats, with proper acknowledgement and source lists.

forPractitioner.text: Teach students to search for and synthesise information in many formats and to acknowledge and list their sources properly.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn to find and combine information from many kinds of source and to credit and list your sources properly.

statements.paraphrase: Carrying out competent study and learning under one's own direction.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' capacity for competent self-directed study.

forBeneficiary.text: You will build your ability to study and learn well on your own.

statements.about: health and safety and EDI at work
statements.paraphrase: Grasping why health and safety, and equality, diversity and inclusiveness, matter in the workplace.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure students learn why health and safety and equality, diversity and inclusiveness matter at work.

forBeneficiary.text: You will come to understand why health and safety, and equality, diversity and inclusion, matter in a workplace.

statements.paraphrase: Valuing and taking part in current debates on sustainability, employability and global perspectives, decolonisation and anti-racism among them.

forPractitioner.text: Give students room to engage with live debates on sustainability, employability and global outlooks, decolonisation and anti-racism among them.

forBeneficiary.text: You will have the chance to take part in current debates about sustainability, careers and global perspectives, including decolonisation and anti-racism.

statements.paraphrase: Seeing the need to act sustainably and to behave and conduct oneself ethically.

forPractitioner.text: Help students see why sustainable action and ethical conduct matter, and give them chances to practise both.

forBeneficiary.text: You will come to see why acting sustainably and behaving ethically matter, and practise both.

statements.about: communicating language knowledge to policy stakeholders
statements.paraphrase: Conveying knowledge about language with authority and sensitivity to those responsible for policies where language matters.

forPractitioner.text: Give students practice in communicating subject knowledge with authority and sensitivity to policy stakeholders for whom language is central.

forBeneficiary.text: You will practise explaining what you know about language, clearly and sensitively, to people who make policies where language matters.
